cd-into-folder.title: Move Into a Folder
cd-into-folder.bodyMarkdown:
`cd` means **change directory**. It changes the terminal's current working directory; it does not move or rename the folder itself.

Suppose you are here:

```text
$ pwd
/home/zoe/projects
```

and `ls` shows a folder named `website`. You can enter it with:

```text
$ cd website
$ pwd
/home/zoe/projects/website
```

The name `website` works because that folder is directly inside the current directory. After `cd`, commands that use relative names will start from the new location.

Think of `cd` as changing your point of view in the filesystem: the files stay where they are, but your terminal is now working from a different folder.

cd-up-one-level.title: Move to the Parent Folder
cd-up-one-level.bodyMarkdown:
Every directory except the filesystem root has a **parent directory**: the folder one level above it. In a relative path, `..` is the special name for that parent.

Suppose your current directory is:

```text
/home/zoe/projects/website
```

Running:

```text
$ cd ..
$ pwd
/home/zoe/projects
```

moves the terminal up exactly one level, from `website` to `projects`.

The two dots are not a folder you created, and they do not mean "go home." They mean "the parent of my current directory." If you are unsure where that will take you, run `pwd` before and after the move.

relative-paths.title: Navigate With Relative Paths
relative-paths.bodyMarkdown:
A **relative path** describes a location starting from the current working directory. Because the starting point is already known, you do not have to type the full path from the top of the filesystem.

Suppose `pwd` shows `/home/zoe/projects`, and inside `projects` there is a folder `site` containing `assets`. You can move through both levels and then inspect the destination:

```text
$ cd site/assets
$ ls
icons  logo.svg
```

`site/assets` is relative because it starts from the current directory and has no leading `/`. The `cd` command changes into that nested location, and `ls` confirms what is inside after you arrive.

Relative paths depend on where you start. Check your current location first when the same path name could exist in more than one place.
